sections.text: A trait describes something a type can do. It mostly lists method signatures (it can also list types; you will meet one with Iterator in Unit 8), and any type can promise to provide them. You have already met one: Display is the trait for "can be shown with {}". Now you will write your own.

trait Speak { ... } defines the trait. Inside, a method signature ending in a semicolon is required: every type that wants the trait must write its own body. A method with a body is a default method: types get it for free, and may override it. impl Speak for Dog gives a type the trait.

Dog only wrote name and sound, and got intro for free. Robot wrote its own intro, which replaces the default. Inside a trait, self.name() calls another method of the same trait; this works for every type that implements it. Dog and Robot are unrelated types, but both can Speak.

This is the same shape as the impl fmt::Display for LoginError you saw, and the one for ShopError you wrote, in Unit 6. Display is a trait from the standard library. It asks for one method, fmt, and the {} in println! calls it. Here it is again for a new type:
Once a type implements Display, Rust also gives it a to_string method for free. That is the power of traits: implement one small thing and get more.
A trait is a promise. impl Speak for Dog is a signed promise that Dog has every method Speak lists. If you forget a required method, the compiler tells you which one.

Traits are like interfaces in Java, C# and Go. Like Java and C# interfaces (and unlike Go's), they can have default methods. Unlike Go, a type must say impl Trait for Type explicitly. Unlike Java, you can implement your own trait for a type from someone else's crate, such as i32 or String. The orphan rule keeps this safe: you may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is defined in your crate. That is why you can't implement Display for Vec<i32> yourself.

exercise.prompt: The starter has a Speak trait with a required speak method and a default shout method. Dog already implements it, and main already prints robot.shout(). Make Robot speak too: its speak should return beep followed by a space and its id. It should print two lines: WOOF, I AM REX and BEEP 7.

tests.label: A Robot with id 7 speaks beep 7
A Robot with id 7 shouts BEEP 7
The program prints the dog and the robot shouting
an id a hard-coded 7 would not match
Dog keeps working
tests.code: check_eq!(Dog { name: String::from("Rex") }.shout(), "WOOF, I AM REX");

hints: Dog gets the Speak trait from its own impl block. Robot needs one too. Which method does the trait require, and which one do you get for free?
Write impl Speak for Robot { ... } and put only the required method speak inside it. It returns a String. Use format! to join beep, a space and self.id.

main already creates a Robot with id 7 and prints robot.shout(), the same way it does for the dog. Once Robot implements Speak, that line works. The whole impl is: impl Speak for Robot { fn speak(&self) -> String { format!("beep {}", self.id) } }

quiz.question: In a trait, what is a default method?
options: A method with a body in the trait, which types get for free and may replace
A method that Rust calls automatically when a value of the type is created
A method with no body, which every type must write for itself

quiz.question: Which line gives the type Robot the trait Speak?
After you implement Display for a type, what else can you do with it?
options: Print it with {:?} and compare two values with ==
Print it with {} and call to_string on it
Copy it instead of moving it, and print it with {:?}
